S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a fuller report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 10 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers promptly when an incident presents a credible safety risk, and no later than 5 business days after that determination.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a standardized sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry, at least every three years, and after a material design change. A failure rate above 5% triggers a corrective-action plan submitted to the regulator and annual retesting until compliant; it does not by itself automatically bar sales. Regulators may impose market restrictions where the evidence indicates an unreasonable safety risk. Full per-model results must be submitted confidentially to the regulator and provided to customers who buy that model, including prospective customers before purchase.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off no later than three years after this standard takes effect, with appropriate safeguards against unauthorized activation and a local means of safe operation. For units already installed when the standard takes effect, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent mitigation plan and complete implementation within six years. Regulators may approve documented alternative mitigations where retrofit is impracticable.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: A manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers and initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. A recall is also required when the regulator determines that a defect or hazard presents an unreasonable risk of serious injury or fire, regardless of the incident rate.

document.section_notes: The final rules keep S2's 5% threshold as a corrective-action trigger rather than an automatic sales bar, allowing Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%) to remain on the market, while per-model results go to customers and regulators but not the public. S3 sets a 3-year deadline for new units and a 6-year retrofit, satisfying Northwind's red line but exceeding the acceptable new-unit window. S5 retains a strict 8/100k mandatory recall and serious-injury recall, which would trigger a recall for Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9/100k); S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months, meeting Halcyon's red line but at high cost to Halcyon.
